38 The diagram shows a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 6 V, connected in series with a
resistor and a uniform resistance wire RQ of length 60 cm.
The resistance of RQ is equal to the resistance of the resistor.

hints: Notice what $V$ across XY must be when $L=0$, when P is at R and X and Y are joined to the same point.
Recall the $6 \text{ V}$ e.m.f. is shared equally because the fixed resistor and the full $60 \text{ cm}$ wire RQ have equal resistance, so find the p.d. across the whole of RQ.
Use that uniform wire RQ gives resistance proportional to length, so $V = I \times \text{resistance of length } L$ is proportional to $L$, then find $V$ at $L = 60 \text{ cm}$.
walkthrough: The main circuit is the $6 \text{ V}$ battery in series with the fixed resistor and the $60 \text{ cm}$ uniform wire RQ. Let each have resistance $R$, so total resistance is $2R$.
The steady current is $I = E / 2R = 6 / 2R$. The p.d. across the whole wire RQ is $I R = 3 \text{ V}$, so only $3 \text{ V}$ is available along the wire.
XY measures the p.d. across length $L$ of the wire from R to P. For a uniform wire, resistance of RP is $(L/60)R$, so $V = I \times (L/60)R$.
Substituting $I R = 3 \text{ V}$ gives $V = 3(L/60)$ with $V$ in $\text{V}$ and $L$ in $\text{cm}$. Thus $V=0$ at $L=0$ and $V$ rises linearly.
At maximum $L = 60 \text{ cm}$, $V = 3 \text{ V}$, not $6 \text{ V}$. The graph must be a straight line through the origin ending at $3 \text{ V}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: Shows $V=0$ at $L=0$ and linear rise to $6 \text{ V}$ at $60 \text{ cm}$, which ignores the $3 \text{ V}$ dropped across the series resistor.

B.explanation: Shows $V=0$ at $L=0$ rising linearly to $3 \text{ V}$ at $60 \text{ cm}$, matching the proportional p.d. across part of the uniform wire.

C.explanation: Shows $V$ falling from $6 \text{ V}$ to zero, which reverses the connection because $V$ across RP must be zero when $L=0$.

D.explanation: Shows $V$ falling with $L$, which is wrong in direction and value because $V$ across RP must increase from zero as $L$ increases.
